PRISON LOVE STORIES

By: Ntokozo Miya | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A loving partner, a fairytale wedding and a family – what most people wish for. But what would make someone with such dreams decide to date an inmate serving a long sentence? We investigate.

Unique Selling Point:
We speak to Tshidi Monkoe who fell in love with an inmate and remained in that committed relationship for four years. She gives us a front-row seat into her life as the girlfriend of an inmate, highlighting the highs and lows, as well as the eventual breakdown of the relationship. We also speak to others who share their unique prison love stories.

Summary:
Tshidi Monkoe was 23-years old when she married the love of her life. Her husband, with whom she has a daughter, became abusive. She filed for divorce three years later. Tshidi then got a job at as a service agent at an office about a month after her divorce.

One day, the colleague who sits next to her had left her desk but her phone rang incessantly. Thinking it might be a client, Tshidi answered the phone, thinking she'd take a message and pass it on to her colleague. That call would change Tshidi's life – the man on the other end was the brother of Tshidi's colleague and also, an inmate serving a 17-year sentence for robbery. Tshidi and the man began frequently speaking to each other on the phone and planned to meet in person.

Tshidi was initially skeptical about getting into a relationship with an inmate but did not have time to consider what could go wrong because it didn't take long for her to fall madly in love.Meeting him in person confirmed this. And so began a 4-year long love affair during which they were even engaged.

However, his release brought about a change in him that destroyed their relationship.

Tshidi speaks to us about the honeymoon phase of their love affair and takes us to the moment they broke up after the inmate was released, and struggled to adjust to life on the outside.

Further information:
Over and above the case study interviews, we also speak to the Department of Correctional Services to understand the policies that impact prison love affairs; and the reason behind those policies.

PRISON LOVE STORY


ACT 1
1
It’s a dog-eat-dog world: 240 prisons that make up the South African prison system. 
On any given day, over 161-thousand inmates call it home.
Almost a third, still awaiting their day in court. 
Over 97% …male. 
For inmates working with the system to rehabilitate themselves, overpopulation, lack of privacy, & gangsterism…can make it a battle until they can rejoin society.
2
It was a world Tshidi Monkoe knew nothing about when she worked as a call-centre operator in Pretoria a decade ago. But it became a rollercoaster ride that propelled her into writing a book.
TSHIDI MONKOE – AUTHOR: My colleague's phone rings, so I pick up the call from my desk, and the man on the other side of the line introduces himself as my colleague's brother.
MAC – On that phone call, he charmed you?
TSHIDI: He really charmed me. He charmed me a lot. 
3
He called her regularly at work…attention she was craving…as her own marriage was falling apart…
TSHIDI: I was separated from my husband who was abusive in many ways. I left him on the night he almost killed me in the presence of our daughter.
TSHIDI: I was enjoying the emotional bandages that I'm receiving from this guy, this love, this affection. 
After two months Tshidi asked him to drop by her work.
Then came the bombshell
TSHIDI: That is when he divulged that I wouldn't be able to come because I'm in prison.
MAC: What goes through your mind when you hear it?
TSHIDI: SO what did he do? What the nature of crime did this guy commit? I didn't want to ask him on the phone because I didn’t want to come across as if I was judging him so I went to the sister …Then asked if he murdered or rape anyone. She said no.. then for me it was a relief.
4
Tshidi had fallen for a convicted armed robber… serving year-four of a seventeen-year sentence. 
He asked her to visit … in maximum security.
TSHIDI: I'm wearing my stilettos while I'm wearing my cousin's clothes. [00:15:10.29] Looking good, like I was walking into the union buildings to meet the president. 
6
LINK - Never in her wildest dreams did Tshidi ever think that she would fall in love with a convicted criminal, let alone be in a committed relationship with an inmate but that's precisely what happened.
7
As with many couples, Tshidi’s journey illustrates how vulnerable abuse victims can be when seeking relationships to regain control. Clinical psychologist Dr Kgamadi Kometsi works with prisoners…
DR KGAMADI KOMETSI – CLINICAL PSYCHOLOGIST: There would be a temptation to explore a situation where a woman is in power ... with a man who is relatively vulnerable, by being incarcerated.
8
Soon, Tshidi lived for her visits to maximum security…
TSHIDI: I bought his favorite stuff. … a book or a photo frame. ... I buy his favorite snacks. I received roses from this man on Valentine's Day. I received chocolates.  
Only sometimes did she wonder if it was all too good to be true.
10
LINK - Prison is a very lonely place so it's no surprise that inmates spend most of their time trying to connect with people on the outside.
11
But are these connections real? 
[GAP]
Until 2018 Thato Molefe spent 20 years inside.
MAC: 00 56 For those 20 years where were you?
THATO: Sun City - the Dragon City… It’s tough in there. The first year is the worst because you don't even understand the lingo.
Thato had a girlfriend on the outside.
THATO: I was very bored and I went onto social media - you think a lot about your real girlfriend and what she’s up to.. Sometimes she’s not able to visit and support you because she doesn’t have the means.. 
In prison, cell phones are officially forbidden - but Thato says it’s an open secret that phones get in and are highly prized - not least for conducting relationships.
THATO: Inmates end up on Facebook, chatting to people. Suddenly you have someone who will visit you… She visits and brings you stuff. She will also bring you lunch.
12
DR KOMETSI: If you find yourself incarcerated, we hope that the experience is so extreme and significant that it will change you…that hopefulness of a woman that is on the outside…you’ve learned your lesson and you will come out of prison being the best person you can be.
13
The prison system welcomes relationships. Singabakho Nxumalo is the spokesperson for Gauteng Correctional Services.
SINGABAKHO: An inmate with a positive support system is easy to rehabilitate because he knows that when he is done with rehabilitation, there will be family waiting for him.
A surprising number of people look for relationships with inmates - online communities show groups for every flavour of relationship from prisons near and far.
But besides emotional support, inmates also foster romantic relationships for practical reasons…
DR KGAMADI KOMETSI: when they apply for parole, they need someone that will sign for them and sometimes their families have denounced them, they don’t want anything to do with them. 
14
For two years Tshidi's man courted her with gifts from behind prison bars - he was still earning rental income from a property outside. Tshidi divorced her estranged husband…and during one prison visit, a surprise waited. 
TSHIDI: He goes down on both his knees, takes out the ring, and then he puts the ring on my finger.
15
Provided some stringent checks are in place, the department does facilitate jailhouse weddings, but they are few and far between, hinting at the fact these connections may be more functional than romantic…
SINGABAKHO: just this financial year alone we only had six with one application pending.
Tshidi was not keen on a jailhouse wedding, but she was the signee, when her man eventually applied for parole.
TSHIDI: When we got engaged, everything was so perfect. 
16 
Act 3
17 
Thato got his freedom in 2018…and broke off his online relationships. He’s trying to build a life with the woman who waited for him.
18
2018 was also the expiry date for Tshidi’s fairytale – her man’s release, that she hoped would be the beginning of their life together – turned out to be the beginning of the end. 
TSHIDI: He was on the phone all the time. He would take his calls outside. Women would be calling him, texting him. He was just busy. 
The penny dropped. 
TSHIDI: I regretted waiting for him. I regretted the things that I did for him, and he also became very emotionally and verbally abusive. ... During this mess, I discovered that I was pregnant
19
After five years Tshidi sought her own release from the relationship.
20
MAC: If your child were to come to you, and would be in the same situation, what would you say to them?
TSHIDI: I would talk her out of that. When a man is behind bars, he's broken. ... And then now you come into the picture as a woman, as a vulnerable woman. Even if he may love you or has go lol od intentions, it is all coming from a broken place. 
21
Personal relationships are not easy at the best of times, but for those imprisoned by their pasts, it’s a high wall to scale.
PROMO 1

VO – All kinds of like-minded people gather on social media – but some groups are more intriguing than others...

THATO MOLEFE – Sometimes inmates end up on Facebook chatting with people. 

VO – And they are looking for more than just friendships.

THATO MOLEFE – The women complain about not having partners. When you chat with them, you open up to each other.

PROMO 2

VO – Gangs, violence and abandonment – things that come to mind at the mention of prison. But here, some people find comfort and companionship. We examine prison romance. 

PROMO 3

VO – Having escaped an abusive husband, a Gauteng woman was desperate for comfort and attention.

TSHIDI MONKOE - He had this laughter that could cure any type of mental illness, and I needed that.

VO – And she found this in the most unlikely person.

TSHIDI MONKOE - That is when he divulged that I wouldn't be able to come because I'm in prison.
